prompt: A city is deciding whether to build a new public swimming pool. The candidate's framework: (1) The pool's opening-season marketing campaign; (2) Expected visitors and fees; (3) Construction cost; (4) Annual running costs; (5) Health and youth programs the pool would support. What is the flaw in this framework?

options.text: Bucket 1 doesn't belong: promotion won't decide whether to build
options.feedback: Right. Promotion matters once the pool exists, not for the decision to build it. Drop it; the other four buckets cover the decision.

options.text: Buckets 3 and 4 overlap: a cheaper build means higher running costs
options.feedback: Build quality affects running costs, but one-time and yearly costs are separate buckets.

options.text: Missing: lifeguards, heating and upkeep each year
options.feedback: Those are annual running costs, bucket 4.

options.text: It's a generic investment case, but a public pool isn't meant to make money
options.feedback: The framework weighs community benefit (bucket 5) alongside usage and costs, which is right for a city decision. The flaw is bucket 1.

explanation: A public investment weighs usage, costs and community benefit, and this framework covers all three. How to market the pool comes after deciding to build it.

extras.corrected_framework: Usage and fees; construction cost; running costs; community benefits
